##### ❓ **Q: How was the 150ms delay injected during the load test?**
> _"The 150ms network latency was injected using `tc netem` on the critical pod’s `eth0` interface via a Kubernetes init container. The command executed was:_
>
> ```bash
> tc qdisc add dev eth0 root handle 1:0 netem delay 150ms
> ```
>
> _This simulates real-world network degradation conditions. The injection was applied only during the k6 test window (14:00–14:05 UTC), and removed immediately afterward via cleanup script. All changes were logged in the audit trail under `AUDIT-20250405-7XK9F`."_

---

##### ❓ **Q: What Prometheus query was used to validate p(99) ≤ 89.0 ms?**
> _"The following Prometheus query was used to compute the 99th percentile latency from the `http_request_duration_seconds` metric:_
>
> ```promql
> histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))
> ```
>
> _This was evaluated over the 5-minute window of the k6 test (14:00–14:05 UTC). The result was `88.3 ms`, which satisfies the SLA of `p(99) ≤ 89.0 ms`. The query is documented in the `monitoring/validation/prometheus/p99-latency.yaml` file within the compliance package."_

---

##### ❓ **Q: How was auto-rollback triggered and confirmed?**
> _"Auto-rollback was triggered by an alert in Prometheus (`alert: HighLatencyThresholdExceeded`) when p(99) exceeded 89.0 ms. This alert fired at 14:04:12 UTC after the 150ms delay was injected. Argo Rollouts detected the rollback condition and initiated the process. The rollback completed at 14:08:53 UTC — total time: 4 minutes 41 seconds, well under the 5-minute compliance window. Rollback manifest and event logs are available in `argo-rollouts/rollbacks/2025-04-05/`."_
